title: Parameters
jupyter: python3

The parameters of a model are the numbers in it: transmission rates, durations, shares, and the like. This page covers where they live, their units, how to name them so they can be documented, changed, and fitted, and the forms a value can take: a number, a value for each group, a value that changes over time, or one that varies between people.

## Values live in the model

In a declared disease, a value lives where it is used. There is no separate block of parameters to fill in: each number becomes a parameter, named after its role:

```{python}
import starsim as ss
ss.options(jupyter=True)

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

measles.pars
```

The number that multiplies a source of infection is `beta`, and a duration is `dur`; where two would have the same name, the transition's name is added (`dur_onset`, `dur_recovery`). What a number means is given by where it is: after `@` and multiplying `I`, a rate; as `init_prev=`, a share of the population.

## Units of time

A typed value says its unit: `ss.days(8)` is a duration, and `ss.perday(1.9)`, `ss.peryear(0.02)` are rates. A bare number takes the unit of the model, which is the unit of its typed values: here days, from `ss.days(8)`, so β = 1.9 is per day. The rates of births and deaths don't count, so adding births per year to this model leaves β per day. A model whose other typed values are in different units (a duration in days and another in years) has no single unit for its bare numbers, which is an error that asks for `unit=`; giving every rate a type avoids it.

Values are converted to the time step of the sim, whatever it is, so the same model can be run with a step of a day or a week. A rate (`ss.perday`) is a rate, converted exactly. A probability over a period, such as a 10% chance of recovering each day, is written `ss.prob(0.1, 'day')`, and is converted as a probability: over a week it is 1 − 0.9^7, not 0.7. See [Time](running_time.qmd) for durations, rates, and dates.

## Named parameters

When a parameter is to be documented, reused, or fitted, give it a name with `ss.par()`. It behaves like its value in a rate, so it can be used anywhere a number can:

```{python}
beta = ss.par(1.9, bounds=[1, 3], doc='Transmission rate per day', source='Chosen to give R0 of about 15')
dur  = ss.par(ss.days(8), bounds=[ss.days(6), ss.days(10)], doc='Infectious period', source='About 4 days either side of the rash')

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ beta*I
recovery  = I >> R @ dur
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

measles.pars
```

- The name is taken from the variable (`beta`), or given with `name=`.
- `bounds` is the range of plausible values. A parameter with bounds can be fitted: `sim.fit()` fits every parameter that has bounds to every result that has data ([Calibration](calibration_fitting.qmd)). A value outside its bounds is an error.
- `doc` (what it means) and `source` (where the value came from) are free text. `describe()` shows them under the transition that uses the parameter, and they are kept when the model is saved.
- `prior=` gives a distribution of belief about the value, used only in calibration ([Gradients and likelihoods](calibration_gradients.qmd)).

```{python}
sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50))
sim.describe()
```

## Changing a parameter

A parameter can be changed when the sim is made, by name, without changing the model. This is how a set of values for one setting, or a fitted set, is used:

```{python}
sim = ss.Sim(measles, pars=dict(beta=1.5), total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50))
sim.run()
print('R0 with beta = 1.5:', round(sim.diseases.measles.R0(), 1))
```

With several modules, a parameter's name is given with its module's, e.g. `pars={'measles.beta': 1.5}`. A name that matches no parameter is an error, which lists the names there are, so a misspelled parameter is never silently ignored:

```{python}
try:
    ss.Sim(measles, pars=dict(betta=1.5)).init()
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e).__name__, e)
```

A parameter can also be changed during a run, from a date or when a condition holds, with `ss.change()` and `ss.modify()`; see [Changing parameters](interventions_changes.qmd).

## The forms a value can take

Where a value is given decides what it means; the form it takes is free. Each of these can be a rate, a duration, a share, or a starting value:

| Form | Example | Means |
|---|---|---|
| A number | `1.9` | The same for everyone, always (in the model's unit of time) |
| A typed value | `ss.perday(1.9)`, `ss.days(8)` | The same, in its own unit |
| A value for each group | `ss.by(age=[2.5, 1.9, 1.0])` | One value for each age group (or other group) |
| A time series | `ss.timeseries({'2025-01-01': 1.9, '2025-03-01': 1.2})` | Changes over time, from given values |
| A seasonal cycle | `ss.seasonal(mean=1.9, amplitude=0.2, peak='March')` | A yearly cycle around a mean |
| A function of the sim | `lambda sim: 1.9 if sim.now < ss.date('2025-03-01') else 1.2` | Worked out at each step |
| A distribution | `ss.lognorm_ex(mean=ss.days(8), std=ss.days(2))` | Varies between people |
| A function of the sim and the people | `lambda sim, uids: ...` | One value for each person (agents only) |

Any of these can be wrapped in `ss.par()` to give it a name, bounds, or a source. The sections below cover each kind.

### Values for each group

`ss.by()` gives a value for each level of a stratification. Here children (0–14) are the most likely to be infected, and older adults the least:

```{python}
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ ss.by(age=[2.5, 1.9, 1.0])*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)
measles.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1}) # Ages 0-14, 15-64, and 65+, with the share in each

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50), verbose=0)
sim.run()
sim.results.measles.infection.by('age').plot()
```

The values can also be given by label (`ss.by(age={'0-14': 2.5, ...})`), as a table, or for several dimensions at once. See [Stratification](models_stratification.qmd#values-by-group). They can also come from code, as a function of the sim that gives one value per level, worked out at each step: `ss.by(patch=fn)`, e.g. a biting rate in each place from mosquitoes written as code, whatever other dimensions the sim has.

## Parameters over time

Contact patterns, reporting, and treatment change over time, and so do the parameters that stand for them. There are three ways to say how.

**A time series**, `ss.timeseries()`, gives the value at some times, and holds each until the next (or, with `mode='linear'`, interpolates between them). With `period=`, it repeats. Measles in children spreads mostly at school, and its epidemics have long followed the school year. Here, in the endemic measles model of [Diseases](models_diseases.qmd#births-and-deaths-in-a-disease), β is higher during school terms than in the summer holiday, with the same mean over the year:

```{python}
def make_measles(beta):
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    return ss.Disease(
        infection = S >> I @ beta*I,
        recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8),
        births    = ss.birth(S, rate=ss.peryear(0.02)),
        deaths    = ss.death(rate=ss.peryear(0.02)),
        init      = dict(S=0.07, I=0.0001),
        name      = 'measles',
    )

terms = ss.timeseries({
    '2000-01-01': ss.perday(1.97), # School term
    '2000-07-20': ss.perday(1.37), # Summer holiday
    '2000-09-01': ss.perday(1.97), # School term
}, period=ss.years(1)) # The same every year

scenarios = {'Constant': ss.perday(1.9), 'School terms': terms}
sims = {}
for label, beta in scenarios.items():
    sims[label] = ss.Sim(make_measles(beta), total_pop=1_000_000, start='2000-01-01', stop='2020-01-01', dt=ss.days(1), verbose=0)

msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.results.measles.infection.resample('month').plot()
```

With β constant, the epidemics die down to a steady level. With school terms, they don't: the yearly forcing keeps them going, and after some years of smaller, irregular epidemics, they settle into a large epidemic every other year, as measles did in England and Wales before vaccination.

**A seasonal cycle**, `ss.seasonal()`, is a smooth yearly cycle, `mean × (1 + amplitude × cos(2π(t − peak)))`: `ss.seasonal(mean=ss.perday(1.9), amplitude=0.2, peak='March')` is highest in March, at 1.2 times the mean, and lowest in September. A cycle of another length takes `period=`: `ss.seasonal(amplitude=0.5, peak='April', period=ss.years(0.5))` peaks in April and October, as with two rainy seasons.

**A function of the sim** is worked out at each step, and can use anything the sim knows: the date, the number of people in a state, or a result. Measles spreads too fast for a change partway through to show, so this example is an influenza-like SIR (R0 = 3), whose transmission falls by half from 1 February. Written as a time series and as a function, it gives the same answer:

```{python}
def make_sir(beta):
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    infection = S >> I @ beta*I
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10)
    return ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001, name='sir')

def beta_fn(sim):
    return ss.perday(0.3 if sim.now < ss.date('2025-02-01') else 0.15)

betas = {
    'Constant':    ss.perday(0.3),
    'Time series': ss.timeseries({'2025-01-01': ss.perday(0.3), '2025-02-01': ss.perday(0.15)}),
    'Function':    beta_fn,
}
for label, beta in betas.items():
    sim = ss.Sim(make_sir(beta), total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-07-01', verbose=0)
    sim.run()
    print(label, '- infections:', round(sim.results.sir.infection.sum()))
```

A function returns a typed value (`ss.perday(...)`), so that its unit is known. A time series or a seasonal cycle is better than a function where it will do: `describe()` can print it, and it is kept when the model is saved, while a function can only be run.

## Values that vary between people

A distribution, given as a value, gives each person their own value: `recovery = I >> R @ ss.lognorm_ex(mean=ss.days(8), std=ss.days(2))` gives each person their own infectious period. For durations, a compartmental run represents the distribution with stages; see [Durations](models_diseases.qmd#durations) and [Distributions](models_distributions.qmd).

A function of the sim and the people, `fn(sim, uids)`, returns one value for each person it is given, and can use anything about them. Here the infectious period is longer for children under 5 (a made-up example):

```{python}
def dur_fn(sim, uids):
    age = sim.people.age[uids]
    return ss.days(8 + 4*(age < 5)) # 12 days for children under 5, 8 for everyone else

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I
recovery  = ss.Transition(I, R, dur=ss.constant(dur_fn)) # Each person's own duration, as given
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

sim = ss.Sim(measles, n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(50))
sim.run()
sim.plot()
```

A rate is worked out for the people who could take it at each step (everyone in its source state), so a function in a rate is called for them, every step. Multiplied by a condition, it is called only for the people the condition holds for, and is 0 for the others: with `rate = ss.par(fn, name='infant')*(ss.ppl.age < 1)`, `fn` is given only the children under 1, and need not check their ages itself.

A function that uses `uids`, or anything else about individual people, needs agents, so a model with one runs as agents. Where the same thing can be said by group (`ss.by(age=...)` on a stratified model), it runs under every solver.

A distribution in a rate gives each person their own rate: in `S >> I @ ss.gamma(a=0.5, scale=3.8)*I`, each person has their own transmission rate (the same as `ss.Transition(S, I, rate=ss.gamma(a=0.5, scale=3.8)*I)`). A distribution on its own after `@` is a dwell time; times a state, it is a rate.

## Parameters of modules written as code

A module written as code declares its parameters and their defaults with `self.define_pars()`, and takes the values it is given with `self.update_pars()`. The values it is given are checked against the defaults, so a misspelled name is an error here too. See [Modules written as code](models_code.qmd).

## Pitfalls

- **A bare number in the wrong unit.** A bare number is in the model's unit of time: in a model whose unit is years, `I >> R @ 0.125` is 0.125 per year. Typed values (`ss.perday(0.125)`, `ss.days(8)`) don't depend on it.
- **Changing the model instead of the sim.** To try another value, give it to the sim (`pars=dict(beta=1.5)`) rather than changing the disease, which every sim made from it shares.
- **A distribution as a value or as a prior.** A distribution as a value is variation between people. Uncertainty about a single value is a prior, `ss.par(1.9, prior=...)`, used only in calibration.
- **A function where a time series would do.** A function can't be printed by `describe()`, exported to another framework, or written out as equations.
